The main interface contains a content editor and chat panel on the left, with a block list on the right. Three key features are highlighted: (a) users verify generated code by executing it inline and viewing output directly in the editor; (b) users curate the LLM context by selecting which elements to include through the context manager; (c) users organize tutorials into blocks, each with its own workspace and LLM chat history.

limitations:
### 6.4. Study Limitations

In our user study, we measured confidence based on what the participants self-reported and did not independently evaluate tutorial quality through expert review or reader comprehension. Participants like P5 tied their confidence to sections where they had executed code (“Having run the code [in block] one, I am very confident it’s correct”). However, we acknowledge that code execution only confirms that code runs and does not validate the surrounding prose. We observed that writers appeared to transfer the confidence gained from verified code to the tutorial as a whole. The reported confidence should therefore be read as writers’ perception of their work rather than an indicator of tutorial quality; future work should evaluate quality independently through expert review or reader comprehension studies.

Second, the control condition let each participant use their preferred LLM tool rather than a fixed system. We made this choice to prioritize ecological validity, so the observed differences reflect how dBlocks compares against participants’ habitual workflows. However, comparing against a fixed baseline could isolate the effect of dBlocks’s features.

Finally, each condition was limited to 15 minutes, and participants were already familiar with their preferred LLM tools but received only a brief tutorial for dBlocks. These constraints affected both conditions differently. For instance, P1 spent the entire control condition on environment setup and never succeeded in executing code; with more time, they might have verified it. In dBlocks, P1 and P10 initially forgot to add content to the context, which can be attributed to their limited familiarity with the interface. The benefits of blocks to scope the content may also become more pronounced as tutorials grow beyond what 15 minutes allows. Overall, the shorter familiarity and 15-minute limit likely disadvantaged dBlocks, which makes the observed confidence difference more notable.

## 7. Conclusion

As software engineering as a field adopts LLMs, we need the research community to design and develop tools that make interactions with these models and their outputs better. We investigated one such context in this paper, tutorial creation, where the work now extends beyond writing code and explanations to prompting and evaluating what the model produces. By analyzing interviews with 17 technical writers, we identified requirements for this work and, grounded in human-centered design methods, iteratively developed dBlocks around them. Our evaluation found that these features let writers engage more deeply with the creation process and improved their reported confidence in the tutorials produced. Whether these shifts hold in documentation work in practice, across longer projects and organizational constraints, remains to be tested, but our study offers a starting point for such investigation. We also argue that the requirements generalize beyond tutorial creation to other LLM-assisted SE tasks such as programming, and we encourage future work to build on them when designing tools for these tasks.
